name: Wei Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for your time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you honestly think. Let's begin with a normal working day. What does it look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Wei, 58, and I buy car and van parts, brake pads, filters, batteries, for a regional auto parts distributor. I'm in at seven, I check which parts the garages ordered overnight, and then I'm on the phone to the suppliers. I know all their sales reps by first name. It's mostly phone, a bit of email, and a lot of looking at the stock sheet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like fixing a problem fast, like when a garage's customer is waiting for a clutch kit and I find one two towns over. What wears me out is the stock sheet. It has 40,000 lines and nobody agrees on the numbers. And my mother's care home bills, but that's a different story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's about what I expect. We've had barcode scanners, then the computer system, now this, and the parts still arrive late. I'd tell my fishing friends it's another gadget that will be forgotten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm not worried about the job itself. But money is tight with my mother's care home, about 900 a month. If the firm has a slow year and cuts hours, I'd feel it quickly. So the worry isn't AI, it's the household pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I do, ring my reps, check the stock sheet myself. I'd keep my 300 a month savings and not buy anything new. If they gave me the new software, I'd use the basic bits and ignore the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay, flat even. I'm not afraid. A bit uneasy about money, but that's been the case since last year, not because of AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said money is tight because of your mother's care. How would that change if the firm cut hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to ask my brother to pay a bigger share, and he won't like it. We'd also stop the weekend trips and I'd sell the boat I use for fishing. That boat is about 3,000, so it would cover three months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ignore the new software. What if you were told you had to use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for training, a proper course, not a video. I'm not stupid, I just don't learn from a screen. If Joyce, my wife, wants to help me with it at home, she's quicker than me.

say: I'd say it's **another gadget** and the parts will still arrive late.
I'd tell my fishing friends it will be **forgotten**.
think: My job feels safe, but **money is tight** with my mother's care home at about 900 a month.
A slow year could cut my **hours**.
do: Keep ringing my **reps** and check the stock sheet myself.
Keep saving **300 a month** and buy nothing new.
Use only the **basic bits** of any new software.
feel: **Flat**, not afraid, with a quiet unease about household money.
S0.quote: The worry isn't AI, it's the household pot.
fieldNote: His unease is about the **care home bills**, not AI, a pressure he already carries.
He is **resistant** and would learn only from a proper course, not a video.
Prefers to keep his routine; his **boat** is his emergency fund.

steps.text: Keep phoning the parts reps and checking the stock sheet
Save 300 a month and buy nothing new
Sell the fishing boat if hours get cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see, because I've heard all this before. But I'd also say the stock sheet is exactly what a computer should do, so maybe. I'd tell the garages we're still the people they ring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be worried. Buying, checking and answering customers are the things named, and that's my day. If a program orders brake pads from the cheapest supplier on its own, there's less for me. I'm 58 and I don't use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm for training, an actual classroom with a person, and I'd learn the ordering screens as slowly as I need. I'd also try to keep the awkward suppliers, the ones who only talk on the phone, as my own. And I'd save an extra 100 a month and ask my brother again about mum's costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels uncomfortable, like moving house. I'd be anxious, and a bit embarrassed that I'm behind. But I'd feel I still had time to catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep the awkward suppliers. Why would they stay with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they're old firms that don't answer emails. Old suppliers like Franco at the filter plant only deal with people they know. That's a skill a program doesn't have, at least not yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the firm cut one buyer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm the experienced one and should stay, but the owner might say I'm the expensive one. I'd ask about retirement at 62 with a payout. I don't want a fight, I want a fair deal.

say: I'd say **we'll see**, since I've heard it all before.
I'd tell garages we're still the people they **ring**.
think: Buying, checking and answering customers are **my day**, and a program can pick the cheapest supplier.
do: Ask for **classroom training** with a real person.
Keep the **awkward suppliers** like Franco as my own.
Save **100 more** a month and ask my brother to share costs.
feel: **Anxious** and a little embarrassed about being behind, though I'd still have time.
S1.quote: Old suppliers like Franco at the filter plant only deal with people they know. That's a skill a program doesn't have, at least not yet.
fieldNote: He accepts the **timing** but will learn only through in-person training.
His strategy is **to own the relationships** that software cannot reach.
He will bargain for an early exit at 62 if one buyer is cut.

steps.text: Ask the firm for a classroom course on the ordering screens
Ask for retirement at 62 with a payout if a buyer is cut
Ask my brother to pay more of mum's care costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I can't believe it, because two years is nothing. I'd say that somebody had better have a plan, whoever is in charge. I'd tell my friends we should keep calm and not lose our heads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be scared. My whole job is the kind of thinking work that goes first, and I'd be out within two years with four months in the bank and my mother's care to pay. I don't use AI, so I'd have nothing to show for myself. I'd be 60 with no job and a payment I can't stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything I could, sell the boat, and ask the firm about a package. I'd ask my brother to take over more of mum's costs, and ask the council about care support. I'd probably look for any hands-on job, maybe in a parts warehouse, since robots come later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels terrible. I'd lose sleep. I'd feel like the ground I stood on for thirty years is gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look for a warehouse job. What would you realistically do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pick and pack, or counter work at a garage supply shop. It'd pay maybe a third less. But there's work for hands, and they'd know my name, I've been supplying those places for thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Joyce that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we need to talk about the house and the mortgage, and about whether you can take extra hours. She works part-time in a pharmacy. I'd feel ashamed saying it, but we've always been straight with each other.

say: I'd say **two years** is nothing and somebody had better have a plan.
think: I'd be **out within two years** with four months in the bank and my mother's care to pay.
I don't use AI, so I'd have **nothing to show**.
do: Sell the **boat** and cut everything I can.
Ask the firm about a **package** and the council about care support.
feel: **Terrible**, like the ground I stood on for thirty years has gone.
S2.quote: I'd be 60 with no job and a payment I can't stop.
fieldNote: He expects to lose his job within two years and has **no tool skills** to offer, so alarm is justified.
The **care home bill** is the fixed cost that makes him feel cornered.
His fall-back is hands-on work that the robots reach **later**.

steps.text: Sell the fishing boat and cut every extra cost
Ask the firm for a leaving package
Apply for pick-and-pack or garage counter work
Ask the council about support with my mother's care fees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is better than two, but it's still fast. I'd tell my friends and my brother that we should start now. I wouldn't say much at work, I'd just watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be worried, but I'd see a way. I'd be 63 by 2031, so I could ride it out and leave then. My mother might not need the care home by then, sadly, which would free up money. That's a hard thing to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save more, about 500 a month, and take that classroom course. I'd learn enough to keep my job until 62 or 63. I'd also tidy my files and write down what I know about the suppliers, so I can leave something useful or sell my knowledge as a consultant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels heavy but manageable. I'd feel anxious in the morning and fine by lunchtime. I'd rather have the five years than not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's hard to say that about your mother. Can you tell me more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's 88 and she's slipping. The bills have been going for three years. I love my mother, and I also count the money. Both are true, and I don't enjoy that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you write down about the suppliers, and who for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who's reliable, who lies about lead times, whose price goes up every March. I'd write it for whoever replaces me, but also for me, in case someone pays me to explain it later. Twenty years of that is worth something.

say: I'd say **five years** is better than two, but still fast.
At work I'd say little and **watch**.
think: I'd be **63** by 2031, so I could ride it out and leave then.
My mother's care bills might **end** before then, which is hard to say.
do: Save **500 a month** and take the classroom course.
Learn enough to keep my job until **62 or 63**.
Write down what I know about **suppliers** to sell as consulting.
feel: **Anxious** in the morning, fine by lunchtime, glad of the five years.
S3.quote: I love my mother, and I also count the money. Both are true, and I don't enjoy that.
fieldNote: He is honest about a **painful** link between his mother's care costs and his own planning.
Five years allows a plan to **ride it out** to 63.
Turns his supplier knowledge into a **saleable** asset, an unusual, practical idea.

steps.text: Save 500 a month towards retiring at 63
Take the classroom course on the ordering screens
Write up supplier notes and offer them as paid advice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and I'll be long gone. I'd tell my friends I'd be fishing, not worrying. I'd say the younger ones should get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I retire at 65, seven years from now, and the big change comes after. If my mother's costs end, we'll have more room. I'd feel sorry for the youngsters starting out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as usual, pay off the mortgage bit by bit, and use the tools a little when they're needed. I'd maybe help train the new buyer, Aiden, he's 27, on the supplier side. And I'd plan my retirement: the boat, a trip with Joyce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels pretty calm. I'd have a bit of unease about money for my mother. Other than that, I'd say it's all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you feel sorry for the youngsters. What would you tell Aiden?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn the supplier side, the phone side, because that's where the trust is. And I'd tell him to save, because jobs come and go. It's what I'd say to my own kids, and I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine, but you also said money is a worry. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. I'm fine on the job, I'm uneasy on money while my mother's alive. If her costs go up, ten years of calm could shrink fast. That's the thing I can't control.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a long time and I'll be long gone.
I'd tell friends I'd be **fishing**, not worrying.
think: I retire at **65**, seven years from now, and the big change comes after.
I'd feel sorry for the **youngsters** starting out.
do: Keep working and pay off the **mortgage** bit by bit.
Help train **Aiden (27)** on the supplier side.
feel: **Calm**, with a little unease about money for my mother.
S4.quote: I'm fine on the job, I'm uneasy on money while my mother's alive.
fieldNote: His job is safe in this scenario, but the **care costs** keep him uneasy.
He wants to pass on his **supplier** knowledge to Aiden.
Seven years to retirement gives him a calm outer voice.

steps.text: Keep buying parts until retiring at 65
Pay down the mortgage bit by bit
Teach Aiden the supplier side of buying

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. I'd have no job, no time, and I'd have no skill with the new tools. What would help is a package I can count on, a real classroom course, and my brother sharing my mother's costs. Some help from the council on the care home would take the pressure off.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not stubborn because I'm stupid. I learn slowly and properly, and I'd like people to give me the time. Most people my age would say the same.

headlineQuote: I'm not stubborn because I'm stupid. I learn slowly and properly, and I'd like people to give me the time.
portrait: Wei, 58, buys **car and van parts** for a regional distributor, and he knows every supplier rep by first name.
Centre in outlook and **resistant** to new tools, he never uses AI and learns only from a proper classroom course.
He has about four months saved and pays toward his mother's **care home**, which keeps him uneasy in every world.
His wife Joyce works part-time in a pharmacy, and his **fishing boat** is his emergency fund.
Moods rise with the speed: uneasy in the mild worlds, **alarmed** at two years, anxious at five.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, with no job, no time and no skill with new tools.
whatWouldHelp: A **package** he can count on, a real **classroom** course and help with his mother's care costs.
